aidb_assessment.novelty: Potentially high. The central contribution is not a new trellis code but an agent-aware post-training recipe: model-written-token KL, gradient-derived module losses, probability-banded output precision, and mixed-domain scale tuning. The first-at-this-budget claim is explicitly qualified by the authors and is not independently established by the supplied blocks.
aidb_assessment.rationale: The same-harness BF16 comparisons and reserve-set KL results justify close attention. Adoption should wait for independent reproduction, matched-harness quantized baselines, broader model coverage, and end-to-end memory measurements on actual consumer GPUs.
aidb_assessment.usefulness: High for researchers evaluating low-bit local agents. The study directly tests long-horizon tasks and reports paired uncertainty, storage, and throughput. Immediate production usefulness is narrower because only one model and one optimized GPU path are demonstrated, while full long-context memory and cross-harness comparisons remain unresolved.

executive_summary: NariQ is a trellis-coded post-training quantization recipe that calibrates Qwen3.8-27B on BF16-generated agent traces and emphasizes model-written tokens. In the authors’ harness, its 3.0- and 2.5-bpw files remain statistically level with BF16 on DeepSWE and Terminal Bench while retaining short-task performance; the 2.0-bpw file degrades materially. The controlled same-harness BF16 comparisons are promising, and held-out KL results strengthen the case. However, external quantized baselines use a different harness, only one model is tested, several component studies are confounded, calibration data details are incomplete, and long-context memory remains unresolved. The result merits replication, not yet broad adoption.

assumptions: The second-order expansion around BF16 and the neglect of interactions between module errors are adequate for allocating widths.
Curvature-weighted errors at different trellis widths are sufficiently uncorrelated to interpret the gradient score as the current module loss.
A module’s loss at another width scales proportionally with the trellis code’s measured mean squared error.
Mean BF16 token probability is an adequate proxy for output-row sensitivity.
KL at model-written positions is a useful development surrogate for downstream agent success.
Repository-level exclusion of DeepSWE repositories sufficiently limits calibration-to-benchmark contamination.
key_components: Model-written-token KL: both models receive the complete prefix, but only BF16-generated model positions contribute prediction targets.
Two-sided trellis rounding is retained when it reduces held-out curvature-weighted error sufficiently; nearly all modules use both input- and output-side statistics.

Per-module sensitivity is inferred from gradients at several width assignments, rescaled by measured code error, combined with inverse-variance weighting, and made conservative with a two-standard-error margin.
A dynamic-programming allocator chooses one permitted width per module under an exact storage check. Linear layers are constrained to at least two bits after the one-bit loss estimate failed.

The output layer is partitioned into probability-ranked bands with separate widths; every output band receives at least two bits to protect rare tokens. At the lowest budget, the input embedding is also banded.
Scale and norm tuning mixes coding-agent traces with general math, science, chat, code, and long-document replies.
method.overview: NariQ retains trellis coding but changes the training signal and precision allocation. It constructs BF16-generated agent traces, computes KL only at model-written target positions while retaining tool output in the prefix, estimates per-module loss from gradients, predicts loss across candidate widths using measured trellis-code error, solves a discretized multiple-choice knapsack, bands output rows by predicted token probability, and tunes scales and norm weights on a mixture of coding traces and general replies.

open_questions: How does NariQ compare with every public quantized baseline when all files use the same server, agent, prompts, attempt count, and task snapshot?
Does model-written-token masking outperform an all-token objective when every other quantization and allocation choice is held fixed?
How sensitive are allocations and downstream scores to calibration repositories, trace count, random seeds, and the coding-to-general tuning mixture?
Does the reserve-set KL improvement predict agent-task improvement across models and budgets, or only within this construction pipeline?
Can the 2.0-bpw deficit be recovered without increasing effective storage, and does any recovery generalize beyond the tuning domains?
What is peak end-to-end memory at long context, including vision, KV cache, activations, runtime workspace, and the unquantized multi-token prediction module?

problem.importance: Long-horizon agents accumulate large contexts and many tool interactions, making weight memory important for local deployment. The paper argues that the practical target is consumer hardware with limited memory and that strong short-benchmark scores can conceal severe agent-task degradation.
problem.scope: The study covers post-training quantization of Qwen3.8-27B at 3.0, 2.5, and 2.0 bpw. It evaluates coding agents, terminal tasks, mathematics, visual understanding, multilingual reasoning, offline KL, file size, and single-session generation speed.
problem.statement: Determine whether a language model can be quantized to three or fewer bits per weight without losing long-horizon agent capability, when conventional calibration on short web text and evaluation by perplexity may not represent tool-using behavior.

proposed_experiments.baseline: BF16 plus all available public files in the same effective-bpw bands, served with identical software, agent, prompts, sampling, task snapshot, attempt count, and hardware.
proposed_experiments.hypothesis: Under a fully matched harness, NariQ at 3.0 and 2.5 bpw is non-inferior to BF16 and outperforms same-budget public quantizers on long-horizon agent success.
proposed_experiments.primary_metric: Paired difference in DeepSWE score with a prespecified non-inferiority margin; fully solved task count and Terminal Bench mean reward are secondary metrics.
proposed_experiments.stop_condition: Conclude support only if the confidence interval excludes the non-inferiority margin against BF16 and excludes zero against the strongest matched-budget quantized baseline; otherwise report the hypothesis unresolved or rejected.

proposed_experiments.baseline: A matched NariQ build using all-token KL, with identical traces, trellis codes, candidate widths, storage budget, optimizer, output banding, and scale-tuning data.
proposed_experiments.hypothesis: Restricting KL targets to model-written tokens improves agent performance beyond an all-token calibration objective.
proposed_experiments.primary_metric: Paired DeepSWE score difference, accompanied by reserve agent KL to test whether the surrogate tracks downstream behavior.
proposed_experiments.stop_condition: Stop after the preregistered task set and seeds; accept the mechanism only if the model-token variant improves the confidence-bounded paired agent score without degrading the non-coding benchmark aggregate beyond a prespecified tolerance.

proposed_experiments.baseline: The released 2.0-bpw checkpoint and a scale-and-norm-only retraining control using the same data and compute.
proposed_experiments.hypothesis: The 2.0-bpw quality gap can be reduced through training beyond scales and norms without exceeding the original storage budget.
proposed_experiments.primary_metric: Worst-case BF16-relative deficit across DeepSWE, Terminal Bench, AIME, RealWorldQA, and MGSM, with exact file bpw reported.
proposed_experiments.stop_condition: Stop if the extended-training variant fails to reduce the worst-case deficit on a held-out evaluation while remaining within the original bit budget, or if gains appear only on domains represented in tuning data.

artifacts: The paper states that Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF files are released.
The paper states that inference is available through the authors’ llama.cpp fork.
Benchmark versions, common sampling settings, context window, attempt policies, task counts, and the DeepSWE task-repository commit are reported.
The quantization objective, allocation strategy, output banding, and scale-tuning mixture are described.
reproducibility.assessment: Artifacts for inference appear available, and the evaluation protocol is described more clearly than the complete construction pipeline. Reproducing reported inference may be feasible, but independently rebuilding identical files and auditing every benchmark result would require substantial missing data and configuration. Reproducibility is therefore partial rather than strong.
missing: Exact calibration, development, reserve, general-prompt, and math-prompt datasets or trace files are not supplied in the document blocks.
Trace counts, token counts, repository lists, preprocessing details, and random seeds are not reported.
The precise candidate width sets, budget discretization, optimization schedule, learning rates, tuning duration, and full per-module allocations are not reported.
No executable benchmark commands, environment lockfile, full hardware/software configuration, or raw per-task outputs are provided in the supplied material.
The paper does not report repeated end-to-end quantization runs, independent replication, or uncertainty from calibration and allocation randomness.

results.context: This is the strongest same-harness long-horizon comparison. The uncertainty intervals implied by the reported standard errors do not establish superiority; they support the narrower interpretation that no degradation was detected.

evidence.quote: At 3.0 and 2.5 bpw, our files are level with BF16 on DeepSWE (Table 1).
They solve 47 and 46 tasks against BF16’s 44, and their DeepSWE scores are 84.9% and 84.5% against BF16’s 83.0% (paired by task, +1.9 and +1.5 points, s.e. 3.2 and 3.6).

results.result: On DeepSWE, the 3.0- and 2.5-bpw files solved 47 and 46 tasks versus 44 for BF16, with scores of 84.9% and 84.5% versus 83.0%. Paired differences were +1.9 and +1.5 points, with standard errors of 3.2 and 3.6.

results.context: The results are consistent with parity but are noisy. They should not be interpreted as evidence that quantization improves performance.

evidence.quote: On Terminal Bench 2.1, our 3.0 and 2.5 bpw files score 102% and 96% of our BF16, within noise of it (paired by task, +1.2 and −2.4 points, s.e. 3.5 and 3.2)

results.result: On Terminal Bench 2.1, the 3.0- and 2.5-bpw files achieved 102% and 96% of BF16. Their paired differences were +1.2 and −2.4 points, with standard errors of 3.5 and 3.2.

results.context: This consequential negative result identifies a practical boundary: the recipe’s apparent parity at the two larger budgets does not extend to the lowest evaluated budget.

evidence.quote: At 2.0 bpw, our file solves 33 tasks and scores 75.7%, 7.3 points under BF16 (s.e. 3.3).
our 2.0 bpw file scores 84%, 10.2 points under (s.e. 3.5).
At 2.0 bpw, the largest drop is on AIME, 11.7 points.

results.result: The 2.0-bpw file materially underperformed: on DeepSWE it solved 33 tasks and scored 75.7%, 7.3 points below BF16; on Terminal Bench it achieved 84%, 10.2 points below; on AIME its largest reported non-coding drop was 11.7 points.

results.context: These centrally scored comparisons avoid the agent-harness mismatch and include a reserve set reportedly unused for selection, but KL remains a surrogate rather than an agent-success metric.

evidence.quote: at 2.5 and 3.0 bpw the best published file in each budget group has 1.7–4.9× our KL on every set, with the same or more bits.
At 2.0 bpw, Unsloth’s UD-IQ2_XS, with 0.27 bpw more, is slightly ahead on the math set (0.0819 against 0.0829); we lead on the other sets, by 2.1× on agent KL.

results.result: On held-out offline comparisons, the strongest published files in the 2.5- and 3.0-bpw budget groups had 1.7–4.9× NariQ’s KL on every set despite using the same or more bits. At 2.0 bpw, a competitor using 0.27 bpw more was slightly better on math, 0.0819 versus 0.0829, while NariQ led by 2.1× on agent KL.

results.context: These measurements demonstrate a concrete storage and throughput profile for the authors’ specialized fork and one GPU, not portable performance across consumer hardware or concurrent sessions.

evidence.quote: occupy 10.1, 8.4 and 6.8 GB at 3.0, 2.5 and 2.0 bpw.
At these three budgets, our llama.cpp fork on one RTX PRO 6000 generates 89, 99 and 112 tokens/s at a 4K-token context, and 71, 77 and 85 at 64K, for a single session.

results.result: The text-only files occupy 10.1, 8.4, and 6.8 GB at 3.0, 2.5, and 2.0 bpw. On one RTX PRO 6000, generation reached 89, 99, and 112 tokens/s at 4K context and 71, 77, and 85 at 64K.
